column6: TXTT draft [§13.12: The token is stated not to be an authentication credential and is limited to its Trust Domain, but the source never says whether holding it suffices or defines key/identity binding for use; checked possession, bearer, proof-of-possession, cnf, binding terms]; AIP (Singla) [§21.3, 8.1: Tier 1 tokens without DPoP are plain Bearer (possession suffices), while Tier 2/3 and flagged scopes are bound to the agent key via mandatory DPoP; all named alternatives are specified]; AIP (NVIDIA) [§5.6.1, 5.7: The token is bound to the agent key, tool and arguments (not bearer), but there is no delegated-authority artifact and possession-alone is not discussed]; Token Exch. Ext [§16: Explicitly states that possession is insufficient where live-presenter authorization is needed and binds the token to a key/authenticated actor (also 1.1, 24.5)]; Draft: Deleg. Auth [§4.2 Trust Model: Possession alone is declared insufficient and authority is bound to the leaf cnf.jkt key; all elements of the definition are addressed]; Draft: Atten. Tok. [§4.7 I6: Proof of Possession, 5.1 Rationale: Possession of the token alone is insufficient; authority is bound to the holder key via cnf.jwk and PoP (plus tool/argument and optional audience binding) before use]; Draft: Deleg. SDJWT [§4.2 Optional Key Binding: Key binding is required for intermediate links but optional for the final holder, so possession-only use is possible; no other binding constraints are defined]
column8: Macaroons [I. Introduction: States that macaroons are bearer credentials and that possession is further confined by contextual caveats and holder-of-key third-party proofs]; UCAN [Core: FAQ "What prevents an unauthorized party from using an intercepted UCAN?": UCAN use is bound to the issuer signature key and the audience DID (and invocations are signed), so possession alone is not sufficient]; MCP Auth [Security Considerations §9 Access Token Privilege Restriction: Tokens are bearer tokens bound only to an audience/resource (partial); no key, identity or context binding beyond audience is specified]; A2A [§7.6.3 In-Task Authorization Security Considerations: Recommends (SHOULD only) binding credentials to the originating agent for in-band credential exchange; otherwise credentials are bearer-style and the binding is not specified]; W3C VC [§9.5 Man-in-the-Middle (MITM), Replay, and Cloning Attacks: Only optionally mentions binding to strong authentication or proof of control (and §8.10 admits bearer use), without defining which constraints must be satisfied before use]; ZCAP-LD [§3. Capabilities: Authority is bound to controller keys and invocation must validate against them (also 3.5: authority by possession), answering the possession question]; Biscuit [Introduction: States bearer semantics (possession suffices) and checks can add ambient conditions, but no key or identity binding of the presenter is specified]; SPIFFE [JWT-SVID §7.3 Transport Security: States that a JWT-SVID is a bearer token (possession alone suffices) and that X.509 SVIDs are key-bound, but this concerns identity documents, not delegated authority, and no general possession-assumption statement is given]; W3C DID [§5.3.4 Capability Invocation: Capability use is bound to a verification method (key) listed in the DID document, so not possession alone; the capability artifact format and mandatory binding are left open and the text is an informative example]

column3: Presentation assumptions (how a presenter proves ownership or presents the artifact; presentation recommendations)
column5: • RFC 9449 §9 (DPoP proof presentation) / • RFC 8705 §7 (mTLS client authentication of the presenter) / • RFC 9700 (BCP 240 — presentation recommendations)
column6: Token Exch. Ext [§16: Defines the presentation/proof-of-ownership mechanism (DPoP, alternatives by agreement) and the resource-side validation and challenge handling (Section 21)]; TXTT draft [§12.1: Defines how the token is presented (dedicated header, one token, not Authorization) and validation at the receiver, but no presenter proof-of-ownership mechanism for the token itself (mutual auth in 11.5 covers only the TTS request)]; Draft: Deleg. Auth [§9.9 Binding the DPoP Proof to the Leaf Delegated Authorization Token: Defines how the presenter proves key ownership (DPoP proof, ath over chain, DA scheme) with presentation security rules (fresh proof, nonce, jti replay detection)]; Draft: Atten. Tok. [§5.2 PoP Token Structure, 5.3 Verification: Defines the PoP JWT by which the presenter proves key ownership and its verification, with presentation security rules (jti, iat window, aat_aud binding, stateful tracking in 8.5)]; Draft: Deleg. SDJWT [§4.2 Optional Key Binding: A KB-JWT proof of possession at presentation is defined (optionally, per policy), but presentation-specific security recommendations are not given beyond the RFC9901 reference]; Draft: TxnTok-Agents [§5.8; 5.4: Presentation security is channel-level mutual authentication (MUST §5.8, SHOULD mTLS §5.4); no mechanism for the presenter to prove ownership of the token.]; AIP (Singla) [§9.17, 21.3, 21.6: Presentation scheme (Bearer/DPoP), proof checks (htm, htu, ath, iat, jti, key binding) and TLS transport recommendations are normatively defined]; AIP (NVIDIA) [§5.7, 7.1, 9.3: Presenter proves key ownership by signing each call, presentation via AIP-Token header/_aip field and verification order are defined, with TLS recommendations in 9.3]
column8: UCAN [Invocation: Invocation Payload > Agents > Issuer: Invocations present the capability with a signature by the invoker's key plus the full proof chain, and Core FAQ recommends authenticated, secure-channel delegation]; MCP Auth [Authorization §9.1 Token Requirements: Defines the presentation channel (Authorization: Bearer header, not query string) but no proof-of-ownership mechanism]; ZCAP-LD [§4.1.1 Invocation HTTP Signature: Defines the presentation mechanism and signature-based proof of key control, but security recommendations for presentation are thin (only a SHOULD-have id usable as nonce)]; Biscuit [Authorizer: Deserializing the token: Specifies verification of the token at the authorizer, but no mechanism for a presenter to prove ownership and no presentation security recommendations]; Macaroons [Preparing requests (macaroon verification section): Defines how discharge proofs are bound and presented with the macaroon, with the attack rationale (phishing re-use) as security recommendation]; SPIFFE [SPIFFE ID §3.2 SVID Components: Names proof of ownership by private key and (JWT-SVID §5.2, §7.3) Bearer presentation with confidentiality advice, but presentation to a relying party of a delegation artifact is not specified]; A2A [§7.3 Client Authentication Process: Defines credential presentation per request and mandatory server authentication (7.4) but no proof-of-ownership mechanism or presentation-specific recommendations]; OpenID SSF [§6.1.1 Push Delivery using HTTP: Defines presentation of an authorization header on push delivery and defers authentication schemes (§7.1.1); not a proof-of-ownership mechanism for a delegation artifact]; W3C DID [§5.3.4 Capability Invocation: Gives an example presentation mechanism (signed message) and authentication relationship (§5.3.1), but no normative presentation recommendations]; W3C VC [§4.13 Verifiable Presentations: Presentation to a verifier with a challenge is recommended, but how a presenter proves ownership is left to the securing mechanism and no concrete mechanism is defined]

column3: Transfer and forwarding assumptions (transmission across entity boundaries, protection in transit, recursive forwarding)
column6: Token Exch. Ext [§35: Specifies per-hop exchange instead of forwarding, cross-domain preserve (19) and depth bounds (22), but no explicit in-transit protection requirement for the artifact]; TXTT draft [§12.2: Specifies unmodified downstream forwarding and cross-domain handling (Section 14) but gives no in-transit protection requirement for workload-to-workload token transfer]; Draft: Deleg. Auth [§7.8 Out-of-Band Delivery: Transit protection requirements and downstream re-delegation (max_delegation_depth) are given, but the delivery protocol and forwarding rules are explicitly out of scope and confidentiality is only SHOULD]; Draft: Atten. Tok. [§9. Privacy Considerations: Transit protection is only SHOULD, transport binding is explicitly undefined (1), though recursive onward derivation is bounded by del_max_depth]; Draft: Deleg. SDJWT [§2.2 Terms and Definitions: Onward delegation across holders is described, but there are no rules on transit protection, forwarding limits or boundary crossing]; Draft: TxnTok-Agents [§5.13; 5.4; 3.3: Cross-boundary egress stripping (MUST) and transit protection (SHOULD mTLS §5.4, MUST §5.8) defined; recursive forwarding governed only by SHOULD-level replacement (§3.3), raw propagation tolerated (§5.14).]; AIP (Singla) [§21.6, 10.1, 12.6: In-transit protection and onward delegation via new sub-agent tokens with depth caps are specified, but there is no explicit rule on forwarding the same artifact downstream (only re-issuance and DPoP non-transferability)]; AIP (NVIDIA) [§7.1, 9.3: Transport protection is specified for proxy-registry and proxy-tool-server links, but there are no rules on transfer across entity boundaries or recursive forwarding of the token to other agents]; OAuth 2.1 [§1.5 Communication security: Protection in transit is normative, but rules for transfer across entity boundaries and recursive forwarding to downstream agents are not defined]; Status List [§11 Security Considerations: Only transmission of the Status List Token (§8.1, §8.2 HTTP GET) is covered, with integrity independent of transport; nothing on forwarding of a delegation artifact downstream]
column8: Macaroons [Macaroon concepts: Covers onward delegation and TLS assumed for message exchanges in the examples, but no explicit transfer rules across entity boundaries]; Biscuit [Overview: Describes holder-side attenuation and sealing to stop downstream derivation, but no transmission rules or in-transit protection]; SPIFFE [JWT-SVID §7.3 Transport Security: Requires confidentiality on all hops for transit protection, but entity-boundary transfer rules and recursive forwarding to downstream agents are not defined (only the audience replay example in §7.2)]; UCAN [Core: FAQ "Is UCAN secure against person-in-the-middle attacks?": Sub-delegation to downstream agents and secure-channel advice are given, but transport rules are left to a transport spec (Core: Token Resolution) and no normative in-transit protection is defined]; A2A [§7.6.3 In-Task Authorization Security Considerations: Acknowledges chain forwarding and requires TLS in transit (7.1), but forwarding rules are only SHOULD-level recommendations and not a defined behaviour]; ZCAP-LD [§3.2 Delegated Capability: Re-delegation to other controllers and chain-length limits are specified, but no rules on transport across entity boundaries or in-transit protection (1]; MCP Auth [Security Considerations §9 Access Token Privilege Restriction: Forbids token passthrough and requires HTTPS endpoints (§3), but does not define transfer rules or recursive forwarding across agents in general]; OpenID SSF [§4.1.8 The "aud" Claim: Gives a transmission/disclosure rule between Transmitter and Receivers (and TLS for endpoints in §7.1); no recursive forwarding of delegated authority]; W3C VC [§8.17 Data Theft: Transit protection is advised for holders, but there are no rules on crossing entity boundaries or on recursive forwarding to downstream agents]
column11: RFC gap: partial RFC coverage (protection in transit only); forwarding rules are defined in draft(s) and prior art — RFC adoption pending

column3: Storage and disclosure assumptions (storage, processing, logging, retention, selective disclosure)
column6: Token Exch. Ext [§25: Covers storage, logging, retention and disclosure of evidence (also 24.3, 20, 21) and selective disclosure via Full/Subset/Actor-Only profiles (Section 15)]; TXTT draft [§15.2: Covers logging restrictions (hash or signature-stripped payload) and PII care, but nothing on storage requirements, retention, or selective disclosure of contents]; Draft: Deleg. Auth [§13.6 Logging and Audit, 11 Privacy Considerations: Logging and disclosure rules are given, but storage and retention of artifacts during asynchronous execution are only touched on and selective disclosure is not supported]; Draft: Atten. Tok. [§9. Privacy Considerations: Storage and transmission guidance is given as SHOULD and logging/retention is not covered; selective disclosure is not supported (token encryption out of scope)]; Draft: Deleg. SDJWT [§4.1 Selective Disclosure: Selective disclosure of contents is supported, but storage, logging, retention and transmission requirements are not specified (privacy deferred to RFC9901)]; Draft: TxnTok-Agents [§3.7; 5.13; 3.8: Disclosure to the inference layer prohibited (MUST), egress minimization (§5.13) and restricted audit-log access (§3.8); no storage/retention rules for holders and no selective-disclosure mechanism.]; AIP (Singla) [§21.12: Retention/logging and storage-after-validation rules are specified, but the source does not state whether the artifact supports selective disclosure of its contents]; AIP (NVIDIA) [§10.2, 6.7, 9.4: Log contents, retention (90 days) and access control are specified and arguments are hashed, but token storage and selective disclosure of artifact contents are not addressed]; OAuth 2.1 [§7.1.3.7 Don't pass bearer tokens in page URLs: Covers logging, cookie storage and information disclosure of tokens (§7.1.1.2, §7.1.3.4), but no storage requirements for autonomous/multi-agent execution and no selective disclosure]; Status List [§12.3 Observability of Relying Parties: Addresses retention, caching (§13.7) and privacy disclosure of status data and one-time-use tokens (§12.5.1), but not storage rules for delegation artifacts or selective disclosure of artifact contents]
column8: A2A [§13.4 General Security Best Practices: Covers logging, storage (13.2 SHOULD securely store credentials) and retention of credentials; no selective disclosure and not specific to delegation artifacts]; W3C VC [§8.9 The Principle of Data Minimization: Selective disclosure and storage/retention advice exist (informative), but nothing on delegation artifacts or autonomous/multi-agent logging and processing]; ZCAP-LD [§3.2 Delegated Capability: Gives a storage requirement for revoked zcaps and Appendix B mentions invocation logs, but no general storage/logging/disclosure rules or selective disclosure]; Biscuit [Introduction: Only an incidental storage remark; no requirements for storing, logging or disclosing tokens and no selective disclosure]; Macaroons [Optimizations and Privacy: Optional privacy omission of information in discharges and root-key storage notes; no normative storage/logging rules]; SPIFFE [Workload API §5.1 Profile Definition: Only the handling of SVID key material delivered over the local Workload API is specified; no storage, logging, retention or selective-disclosure rules for delegation artifacts (searched: log, store, disclos, retain)]; UCAN [Core: Implementation Recommendations > Delegation Store: Optional store, eviction and provenance-log guidance and key-handling advice only; no logging, disclosure or selective-disclosure requirements for delegation artifacts]; MCP Auth [Security Considerations §2 Token Theft: Requires secure storage and logging-related protection of tokens by reference to OAuth 2.1; no selective disclosure or multi-agent asynchronous handling is specified]; OpenID SSF [§9.2 Information Harvesting: Addresses disclosure of SET content and PII, but not storage/logging/retention of delegation artifacts or selective disclosure of artifact contents]; W3C DID [§10 Privacy (Personal Data) / §4 Privacy: Addresses disclosure of DID document contents and selective disclosure as a goal; does not cover storage/logging/retention of delegation artifacts]

column3: Replay assumptions (inherent replay resistance or external controls)
column5: • RFC 9449 §9 (DPoP replay resistance) / • RFC 6750 §5 (bearer: no inherent replay resistance, TLS required)
column6: Token Exch. Ext [§24.5: States the token is not inherently protected against use by a presenter, requiring external sender-constraint (16), and Section 20 defines atomic replay controls for proofs]; TXTT draft [§13.1: States the token has no inherent replay resistance and names the external controls (short lifetime MUST, txn-based single-use check in 13.2); R9(e) cross-reference is outside this source]; Draft: Deleg. Auth [§12.4 Delegated Authorization Token Replay: States inherent resistance (key binding) and its limits and the external controls required (DPoP, ath, freshness, replay detection); the R9(e) cross-reference is not a source matter]; Draft: Atten. Tok. [§8.5 Replay Attacks: States inherent resistance (probabilistic, time-window) and the external stateful controls required for side-effecting calls; R9(e) cross-reference is not a source matter]; Draft: TxnTok-Agents [§5.1: States inherent resistance (short lifetime) and external controls (tracking, usage context) but only as a security consideration with SHOULD-level controls.]; AIP (Singla) [§9.6.5, 21.1 (TS-1, TS-7), 9.17: Intercept-and-use threat is named (TS-1, TS-7), inherent resistance is via jti cache and external control via DPoP with separate replay cache; the R9(e) cross-reference is not required]; AIP (NVIDIA) [§5.7 Step 4, 9.6: Per-token nonce cache and timestamp freshness give inherent replay resistance via specified verification steps; the R9(e) cross-reference is not required]
column8: UCAN [Core: Implementation Recommendations > Replay Attack Prevention: Core FAQ covers intercept-and-use and replay, stating that replay prevention is an external uniqueness-tracking control and delegation itself is idempotent]; ZCAP-LD [§4. Invocation: Only a SHOULD-level nonce hint; no discussion of intercept-and-use vulnerability or inherent replay resistance]; Biscuit [Introduction: Identifies bearer nature (replay-able if intercepted) and authorizer ambient checks like time and source IP as external controls, but no explicit replay analysis]; Macaroons [Contextual confinement: Addresses bearer theft vulnerability and external controls (IP, ChannelID, fresh third-party discharges, short-lived discharges)]; SPIFFE [JWT-SVID §7.1 Replay Protection: States the intercept-and-use vulnerability, that no inherent resistance exists, and the external controls (aud, exp, optional jti); the R9(e) cross-reference is not required of the source]; MCP Auth [Security Considerations §2 Token Theft: Acknowledges intercept-and-use risk and relies on external controls (short lifetime, PKCE) rather than inherent replay resistance; no sender-constraint is defined]; A2A [§7.6.3 In-Task Authorization Security Considerations: Addresses use of intercepted/propagated credentials by other agents via an optional binding; no replay terminology or inherent resistance defined (no 'replay' in text)]; W3C DID [§8 DID Method Security Requirements: Requires methods to document replay but defines no replay resistance for capability artifacts; delegates to DID method specs]; W3C VC [§9.5 Man-in-the-Middle (MITM), Replay, and Cloning Attacks: States vulnerability to intercept-and-reuse, that replay resistance is not inherent, and lists external controls (verifier challenge, validity period); the R9(e) cross-reference concerns our own spec]

column3: Derivation and re-delegation assumptions (derivation, recursion limits, no authority expansion)
column6: Token Exch. Ext [§24.4: Defines derivation by extend/preserve (14.2, 19), no scope widening, subset-only narrowing, and bounded chain depth (22, MUST bound chain depth)]; TXTT draft [§13.15: Replacement tokens may not expand authority and re-issuance SHOULD be limited, but the limit on recursive replacement is only a SHOULD tied to lifetime extension, so recursion restriction is not firmly specified]; RAR agent ext [§2.3 Authorization Flow and The Role of Token Exchange: Covers derivation of narrower tokens from an intent token via token exchange with AS-side non-expansion checking (also Section 7 strict constraints), but gives no rule on recursive derivation or re-delegation depth]; Draft: Deleg. Auth [§4.5 Client-to-Client Delegation, 5.3.2 The max_delegation_depth Claim: Derivation by client-issued child tokens is defined, with bounded recursion via depth and mandatory no-expansion rules (4.2, 5.3.3-5.3.6)]; Draft: Atten. Tok. [§4.3 I2: Depth Monotonicity, 4.5 I4: Capability Monotonicity: Derivation from a parent token is defined with bounded recursive depth (I2) and mandatory non-expansion of authority (I4)]; Draft: Deleg. SDJWT [§8.2 Delegation Policy: Re-delegation is enabled by chained KB-SD-JWTs and limits are only optional claims; no normative bound on recursion or rule against authority expansion]; Draft: TxnTok-Agents [§4.2.1; 4.2.3; 5.5: Derivation via replacement flow with MUST rules: immutable sub/txn/aud/act, scope only attenuated, monotonic min_assurance_level (§5.9), recursion bounded by hop_count rejection; all four asked components present.]; AIP (Singla) [§10.2, 9.15, 10.1: Sub-agent derivation is allowed with recursive depth limits (default 3, hard cap 10) and attenuation-only enforcement so derived authority cannot expand]; OAuth 2.1 [§4.3.1 Refresh Token Grant, Token Endpoint Extension: Refresh derives new access tokens without scope expansion, but recursive derivation, exchange and downstream re-delegation are not addressed]
column8: UCAN [Core: Attenuation: Core Security Considerations permit sub-delegation without alerting the delegator, and Attenuation forbids authority expansion]; MCP Auth [Security Considerations §9 Access Token Privilege Restriction: Addresses propagation by prohibiting passthrough and requiring a separately issued upstream token; no derivation/exchange or authority-non-expansion rules are given]; A2A [§7.6.2 In-Task Authorization Client Responsibilities: Describes propagation of authorization requests along agent chains; no constraints on recursion depth or non-expansion of authority]; ZCAP-LD [§2. Terminology: Derivation from a parent is defined with inherited restrictions and normative non-expansion checks (3.2: expiry, allowedAction, invocationTarget not less restrictive; SHOULD limit chain length)]; Biscuit [Overview: Defines derivation by appending attenuating blocks, with scopes ensuring a token cannot increase its rights and sealing preventing further attenuation]; Macaroons [Macaroon concepts: Derivation by attenuation with chained MACs (caveats can only be added) and recursive discharges are specified]; SPIFFE [X.509-SVID §3.2 Signing Certificates: Signing-certificate chains permit derived issuance bounded by pathLenConstraint and name constraints (§4.1, §4.2), but SVIDs carry no delegated authority and no re-delegation or non-expansion rule for leaf SVIDs]; W3C DID [§5.3.5 Capability Delegation: Describes derivation of a capability by signing it over to another subject; no constraints on recursion or non-expansion of authority]

column11: RFC gap: partial RFC coverage (single-hop derivation) — RFC adoption pending

column3: Audience and context restrictions (target components, tool schemas, parent transactions, runtime environments)
column6: Token Exch. Ext [§8: Restricts validity to a single resource (exact match), scope, workflow/acti and predecessor, per hop]; TXTT draft [§9.2: Token validity is restricted to a Trust Domain via aud, and bound to a transaction (txn) and request context (rctx/tctx)]; RAR agent ext [§2.3 Authorization Flow and The Role of Token Exchange: Only describes (non-normatively and negatively) the lack of audience restriction; lifecycle_binding ties validity to an external task but no audience, tool-schema or ambient-context restriction is defined]; Draft: Deleg. Auth [§5.3.5 The aud Claim: Audience (resource server) restriction with downscoping is specified, but tool schemas, parent transactions and runtime environments are not restricted and request/task binding is out of scope (1.3)]; Draft: Atten. Tok. [§3.3 Capability Claims via authorization_details: Validity is restricted to specific tools and argument constraints and par_hash binds to a parent token (4.6), but audience binding is only in the optional PoP aat_aud and no runtime-environment restriction exists]; Draft: Deleg. SDJWT [§8.3 Delegate SD-JWT Revocation: Optional claims can constrain usage of a delegated token, but no defined audience, tool-schema or parent-transaction restriction mechanism exists]; Draft: TxnTok-Agents [§5.8; 3.3.1: aud and txn immutable (MUST §3.3.1) give target and parent-transaction restriction (semantics inherited from base spec); runtime-environment restriction is SHOULD; no tool-schema restriction.]; AIP (Singla) [§9.6.4, 9.17, 9.15: Validity is restricted to the audience, to the request method/URI and token via htm/htu/ath, and to scopes/manifests and approval-envelope steps with action hashes]; AIP (NVIDIA) [§5.6.1, 5.7: Token is bound to a specific tool name and argument hash, but there is no audience, parent-transaction or runtime-environment restriction]; OAuth 2.1 [§7.1.4 Access Token Privilege Restriction: Specifies audience restriction to target components with MUST-refuse verification by the resource server, plus restriction to resources and actions]
column8: ZCAP-LD [§3.2 Delegated Capability: Normatively restricts validity to a specific invocationTarget (plus allowedAction and expires), meeting the target-component restriction]; Biscuit [Authorizer: Checks restrict validity to specific resources, operations and ambient context supplied by the authorizer]; Macaroons [I. Introduction: Caveats restrict validity to context such as time, IP, specific chunk/operation (first-party) or third-party conditions]; SPIFFE [JWT-SVID §3.2 Audience: aud restricts validity to a target service (validators MUST reject otherwise), but nothing on tool schemas, parent transactions or runtime-context restrictions, and scoping is a SHOULD]; UCAN [Delegation: Policy: Restricts validity via sub, cmd and policy predicates plus aud/principal alignment (Delegation: Principal Alignment) and time bounds]; MCP Auth [Security Considerations §9 Access Token Privilege Restriction: Normatively restricts token validity to the specific target component (MCP server) via audience/resource indicator; other listed context types are not needed as the definition is disjunctive]; A2A [§13.2 Push Notification Security: Only SHOULD-level restriction of token validity to a single push configuration; no audience or tool/transaction restriction of delegated authority]; OpenID SSF [§8 Management API for SET Event Streams: Restricts access to streams to specific audience values (target components); not a restriction on a delegation artifact's own validity by tool schema or transaction]; W3C DID [§5.3.4 Capability Invocation: Informatively ties a capability to a resource/action; no normative audience, tool schema or transaction restriction]; W3C VC [§9.5 Man-in-the-Middle (MITM), Replay, and Cloning Attacks: Audience/domain restriction is available only as an option of some securing mechanisms for presentations; no restriction to tool schemas, parent transactions or runtime environments]
column10: ◑·◉  RFC partial + Draft-complete (non-normative — RFC adoption pending)
column11: RFC gap: only component/audience restriction is normative; restriction to tool schemas, parent transactions or runtime environments has partial draft/prior-art patterns only.

column3: Security consequences of artifact compromise (blast radius, failures, remediation, chains across trust domains)
column6: TXTT draft [§7: Mentions blast-radius limitation and mandates short lifetime, but defines no remediation (revocation/isolation) or cross-trust-domain compromise handling for an exfiltrated token]; Draft: Atten. Tok. [§8.1.1 Threats Mitigated, 8.4 Holder Key Compromise, 8.9 Token Revocation: Blast radius and expiry-based mitigation are specified, but revocation/isolation is explicitly out of scope (8.9), so remediation behaviours are not defined]; AIP (Singla) [§11, 11.4, 21.1 (TS-2): Remediation (revocation, recursive propagation, fail-closed live checks, short TTL limiting exposure) across a delegation chain is normatively specified; blast radius is bounded by scope/TTL rather than explicitly analysed]; AIP (NVIDIA) [§9.7, 5.5, 9.2: Revocation and worst-case 60-second exposure are specified and compromised runtimes are listed as out of scope, but there is no blast-radius analysis or delegation chain across trust domains]; OAuth 2.1 [§4.3.1 Refresh Token Grant, Token Endpoint Extension: Covers compromise detection, revocation and impact reduction (§7.1.3.5), but no blast radius analysis for multi-domain delegation chains]; Token Exch. Ext [§24.2: Covers key-compromise consequences and remediation (cutoff, backdating, fail-closed) and cross-domain custody, but not direct blast radius of an exfiltrated token beyond sender-constraint (24.5)]; Draft: Deleg. Auth [§12.3 Compromise of a Client Key: Blast radius (12.3), protocol-level limits of revocation (12.12) and remediation by revocation of a token and its descendant chains (10.4) are all specified]; Draft: Deleg. SDJWT [§8.3 Delegate SD-JWT Revocation: Revocation difficulty and chain mis-matching (8.1) are noted, but blast radius, exfiltration consequences and cross-domain chain remediation are not defined]; RAR agent ext [§7. Security Considerations: Informative note on revocation limiting the window for compromised tokens (with MUST revoke on terminal state in 3.2.1), but no blast-radius, exfiltration-specific or multi-trust-domain chain handling is defined]; Status List [§1 Introduction: Provides a revocation/suspension remediation channel for Referenced Tokens (§1.2 Rationale, §7), but no blast radius, exfiltration failure analysis or multi-domain delegation chain behaviour]
column8: ZCAP-LD [§3.2 Delegated Capability: Mandatory expiry and a revocation endpoint address compromise remediation, but no blast-radius analysis or cross-trust-domain chain handling (revocation section is only a non-normative backlog item)]; Macaroons [Revocation discussion: Discusses revocation strategies and stolen-token mitigation, but no explicit blast-radius or multi-trust-domain exfiltration handling]; Biscuit [Authorizer: Revocation identifiers: Provides per-block revocation identifiers as remediation, but no blast-radius or exfiltration/cross-domain chain discussion]; UCAN [Revocation: Introduction: Core Security Considerations cover blast radius via per-device keys and last-resort downstream revocation, and Revocation: Scope handles transitive chain revocation]; MCP Auth [Security Considerations §2 Token Theft: States blast radius of theft and mitigations (short-lived tokens, refresh rotation) but defines no revocation/isolation behavior or multi-domain chain handling]; W3C VC [§9.8 Device Theft and Impersonation: Describes consequence and mitigations of device theft and key compromise (§9.2), but no blast-radius, revocation/isolation behaviour or multi-domain chain handling]; SPIFFE [X.509-SVID §4.2 Name Constraints: Addresses blast radius for compromised signing certificates (and SPIFFE ID §4.1.1 short lifetimes), but not exfiltration of an individual artifact, revocation behaviour, or multi-domain delegation chains]; A2A [§13.4 General Security Best Practices: Mentions revocation and rotation only as SHOULD-level; no blast radius or multi-trust-domain chain compromise behavior defined]; W3C DID [§9.8 Verification Method Revocation: Covers compromise consequences (attacker use indistinguishable until revoked) and revocation remediation for keys;
